references.text: The Mosaic law stipulates that a newly married man shall not go out to war or be burdened with any obligation, but shall be free at home for one year to bring joy to his wife. The man in Jesus' parable uses his marriage as an excuse not to come to the meal, which recalls this provision in [ref:5 Mos 24:5|Deuteronomy 24:5].

In [ref:5 Mos 20:7|Deuteronomy 20:7], a man who has become engaged to a woman is exempted from military service. This regulation forms the background for the man's excuse in the parable—that marriage is a valid reason for exemption from obligations.

The two previous guests in the parable ([ref:Luk 14:18-19|Luke 14:18–19]) give similar excuses—buying a field and oxen—for not coming to the great meal. All three excuses show how earthly concerns are prioritized over God's invitation.

In [ref:Luk 14:26|Luke 14:26], Jesus says that whoever does not hate his wife and family cannot be his disciple. This emphasizes that even the closest family ties must not stand in the way of discipleship—the same point illustrated by the man's rejection of the invitation because of marriage.

In Jesus' parable about the king's wedding feast in [ref:Matt 22:2-5|Matthew 22:2–5], guests are invited to a banquet, but they do not care and instead go to their fields and business. The parallel to Luke 14:20 is clear: the guests reject the invitation in favor of worldly obligations.

Paul warns in [ref:1 Kor 7:29-33|1 Corinthians 7:29–33] that those who are married have their attention focused on worldly things and how to please their spouse. This sheds light on the theme in Luke 14:20, where marriage becomes an obstacle to responding to God's call.

In [ref:Luk 18:29-30|Luke 18:29–30], Jesus promises that whoever has left home, wife, siblings or parents for the sake of God's kingdom will receive many times more. This contrasts with the man in the parable who lets marriage prevent him from accepting God's invitation.
